keep: The idea is named up front: the column space is everything the matrix reaches, the null space everything it crushes to zero, and the crushed directions are why answers come in whole lines and why it reaches less.

The picture is the brief's two panels: input and output, the column space shaded, the null space dashed, slide along keeping the output still, a target that lights a line of answers on the shaded set and ends in 0 = 1 off it.

One worked example runs through from the rule: [1 2; 2 4] reaches only the line through (1, 2) because (x + 2y) lots of (1, 2); (2, −1) is crushed; (1, 1) and (3, 0) both land on (3, 6); (3, 7) gives 0 = 1; [1 1 1; 1 2 3; 2 3 4] reaches z = x + y, crushes (1, −2, 1), and (6, 14, 20) has the line (1, 2, 3) + t(1, −2, 1).
The side where the cause is absent is shown: [1 2; 2 5] crushes only zero, reaches the whole plane and gives (3, 7) one answer.

The brief's misconceptions each get a screen: every answer is drawn landing on b (5, 11); x read as a mix of columns as well as an input (10); a plane missing the origin as a column space (8); 0 = 0 against 0 = 1 in the practice.

Thirteen screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) and DO (2, 4, 6, 8, 10), ending with two mixed puzzles (12, 13). Four footnotes, each on a definition or rule he might look up, none named in the text. The RCD is a new analogy from his trade.
fix: Causal step skipped: 'each column either adds a new direction or is a mix of the others' fails for [1 2; 2 4], where each column is a mix of the other. Go through the columns in order, each one against those before it.
False absolute in the analogy: 'only current that leaks to earth' moves the RCD reading. Any current that leaves by another path does, such as a borrowed neutral. Say so.
Common mistake too vague: 'Both views give the same answer' does not say what the second view is. Give A(1, −2, 1) = 0 read as a mix of columns adding to zero.

recommendedShape.tradeAnalogyWithBreaks: RCD, with the leak path widened in draft 2
